data.sourceTitle: Magnetic Materials and a Common Misconception
data.targetTitle: Magnetic Materials and a Common Misconception
data.sourcePassage: A magnetic material is a material that is attracted by a magnet. At KS3, the main magnetic materials are iron, steel, nickel, and cobalt. Steel is magnetic because it contains iron. A common mistake is to say that all metals are magnetic, but this is not correct. Copper, aluminium, brass, gold, and silver are metals, yet they are not attracted strongly by ordinary classroom magnets. In a simple test, an iron nail and a steel paperclip are attracted, but a copper coin, aluminium foil, brass key, plastic ruler, and wooden pencil are not. This evidence shows that magnetism depends on the material, not simply on whether an object is a metal.

questions.question: Name two magnetic materials mentioned in the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: Iron and steel are two magnetic materials. Nickel and cobalt are also acceptable.

questions.question: Which statement is best supported by the passage?
questions.modelAnswer: Only some metals are magnetic in classroom tests.

questions.question: Why is steel usually magnetic?
questions.modelAnswer: Steel is usually magnetic because it contains iron.

questions.question: Use evidence from the passage to explain why the statement “all metals are magnetic” is wrong.
questions.modelAnswer: Copper, aluminium, and brass are metals but were not attracted by an ordinary classroom magnet.

questions.question: What conclusion can be drawn from comparing the iron nail with the copper coin?
questions.modelAnswer: The iron nail was attracted but the copper coin was not, so magnetic behaviour depends on material type rather than simply being metal.

data.sourcePassage: Magnets have two poles. The magnetic effect is usually strongest near the poles. The north-seeking pole is labelled N and the south-seeking pole is labelled S. Like poles repel, so N repels N and S repels S. Unlike poles attract, so N attracts S. A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where magnetic forces act. Field lines are drawn models that show the direction and pattern of the field. Outside a bar magnet, field lines leave the north pole and enter the south pole. Where field lines are closer together, the magnetic field is stronger. Field lines should not be treated as real strings or wires, and the field exists in the space around the magnet even where no line has been drawn.

questions.question: What happens when two north poles are placed near each other?
questions.modelAnswer: They repel each other.

questions.question: Outside a bar magnet, field lines are drawn from:
questions.modelAnswer: They are drawn from north to south outside the magnet.

questions.question: What do closer field lines show?
questions.modelAnswer: Closer field lines show a stronger magnetic field.

questions.question: Why is it wrong to say field lines are real wires?
questions.modelAnswer: Field lines are drawn models used to represent an invisible magnetic field; they are not physical objects.

questions.question: A steel paperclip is placed near a pole of a bar magnet. Why might it experience a large force there?
questions.modelAnswer: The field is strongest near the poles, shown by field lines being close together, so the magnetic force is greater.

data.sourcePassage: Induced magnetism happens when a magnetic material becomes a temporary magnet because it is placed in a magnetic field. A steel paperclip touching a strong magnet can become magnetised and may attract another paperclip. This can form a paperclip chain. When the magnet is removed, most of the temporary magnetism is lost. Soft iron shows temporary magnetism strongly because it magnetises easily and loses magnetism quickly. Compasses also depend on magnetism. A compass needle is a small magnetised needle that lines up with the Earth’s magnetic field, so its north-seeking end points roughly north. However, a compass can be affected by nearby magnets, steel objects, electric currents, and electronic devices, so these should be kept away during navigation.

questions.modelAnswer: It lines up with the Earth’s magnetic field.

questions.question: Why is soft iron useful where temporary magnetism is needed?
questions.modelAnswer: Soft iron magnetises easily and loses magnetism quickly when the field is removed.

questions.question: Explain why a compass should be kept away from a strong magnet during navigation.

data.sourcePassage: An electromagnet is a magnet made using an electric current. When current flows through a wire, a magnetic field is produced. Winding the wire into a coil makes the field stronger because the fields from each turn add together. A soft iron core inside the coil can strengthen the electromagnet further. An electromagnet can be made stronger by increasing the current, increasing the number of turns in the coil, or using a suitable magnetic core. In a fair test of coil turns, only the number of turns should change. The same cell voltage, core material, wire type, paperclips, contact time, and switch-on time should be kept the same. The circuit should be switched off between readings because wires, coils, and cells can heat up if too much current flows.

questions.question: What is an electromagnet?
questions.modelAnswer: An electromagnet is a magnet made using an electric current.

questions.question: Why does winding wire into a coil make the magnetic field stronger?
questions.modelAnswer: The magnetic fields from each turn of the coil add together.

questions.question: Which change would usually make an electromagnet stronger?
questions.modelAnswer: Increasing the number of turns in the coil would usually make it stronger.

questions.question: Why must the same cell voltage be used when testing the effect of coil turns?
questions.modelAnswer: Cell voltage should be controlled so only the number of turns changes; otherwise the test would not be fair.

questions.question: Explain one safety reason for opening the switch between readings.
questions.modelAnswer: Opening the switch stops the current and gives the coil, wires, and cell time to cool, reducing the risk of overheating.

data.sourceTitle: Applications: Cranes, Bells, Motors, and Generators
data.targetTitle: Applications: Cranes, Bells, Motors, and Generators
data.sourcePassage: Permanent magnets and electromagnets are useful for different jobs. A permanent magnet is useful on a fridge because it keeps attracting steel without needing a power supply. An electromagnet is better for a scrapyard crane because it can be switched on to lift steel and switched off to release it. Electric bells and buzzers use an electromagnet that repeatedly pulls an iron armature, breaks the circuit, switches off, and springs back to remake the circuit. Relays use a small current to operate a switch in another circuit. Loudspeakers and headphones use changing currents and magnetic forces to make a cone or diaphragm vibrate, producing sound. Motors use electricity and magnetism to produce movement, transferring electrical energy to kinetic energy. Generators and dynamos do the opposite job by using movement and magnetism to produce electricity.

questions.modelAnswer: It keeps attracting steel without needing a power supply.

questions.question: Why is an electromagnet better than a permanent magnet for a scrapyard crane?
questions.modelAnswer: It can be switched on to lift steel and switched off to release it.

questions.question: What does a motor transfer electrical energy into?
questions.modelAnswer: A motor transfers electrical energy into kinetic energy.

questions.question: How does a loudspeaker produce sound at a simple KS3 level?
questions.modelAnswer: A changing current changes magnetic forces, making a cone or diaphragm vibrate and produce sound waves.

questions.question: Compare the basic jobs of a motor and a generator.
questions.modelAnswer: A motor uses electricity and magnetism to produce movement, while a generator uses movement and magnetism to produce electricity.
